content_voiceover: This slide is flagged as a must-know exam topic, so pay close attention. FLT3 inhibitors are classified along two independent axes, generation and type. By generation, sorafenib and midostaurin are first generation TKIs, while quizartinib, gilteritinib, and crenolanib are second generation, generally more potent and more selective. The kinome tree diagrams up top visually show target selectivity, notice how gilteritinib and crenolanib have that distinct blue dot marking a unique kinase target, AXL, which contributes to their activity profile. The second axis is functional type. Type one inhibitors are active against both ITD and TKD, or tyrosine kinase domain, mutations, because they bind the active conformation of the kinase, midostaurin is the first-generation example, gilteritinib and crenolanib are second-generation examples. Type two inhibitors only work against ITD mutations, not TKD, because they bind the inactive kinase conformation, sorafenib is first generation, and quizartinib, bolded here for emphasis, is the key second-generation type two inhibitor. This type one versus type two distinction, and which drugs work against TKD mutations, is exactly the kind of detail that shows up on written boards.
keypoints: FLT3 inhibitors classified by generation, first gen versus second gen
First generation, sorafenib and midostaurin, second generation, quizartinib, gilteritinib, crenolanib
Type I inhibitors hit both ITD and TKD mutations, active conformation binding
Type II inhibitors hit only ITD mutations, inactive conformation binding
Sorafenib is the first-generation type II inhibitor, quizartinib is the key second-generation one
keypoint_voiceover: Two axes to memorize, generation and type. Type one drugs like midostaurin and gilteritinib cover both ITD and TKD mutations. Type two drugs like sorafenib and quizartinib only cover ITD mutations, that gap is a classic board question.
